analysis.one_liner: Taxes corporations to publicly fund House campaigns and caps campaign spending.
analysis.headline: A bill to publicly finance House elections with spending caps never got a hearing or a vote, dying in committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced private campaign donations with public funding for House elections, capping how much candidates could spend based on their district's income. It would ban 'soft money' contributions and large donor committees, and pay for the new funding through taxpayer checkoffs and a slight increase in the corporate tax rate. It never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters would benefit from candidates who no longer depend on large donors and corporate contributions to win House elections, aiming to reduce the influence of wealthy donors over Congress. The public funding mechanism relies on voluntary taxpayer checkoffs and an additional 0.1% corporate tax on income over $10 million, meaning taxpayers and corporations foot the bill for the new system rather than campaign donors directly.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes the 'Grassroots Good Citizenship Fund' to publicly finance House general elections using Treasury funds rather than private contributions.
Caps campaign expenditures for major, third-party, and independent House candidates at amounts scaled to each district's median household income, with a $1,000,000 ceiling in the wealthiest district.
Bans 'soft money' contributions in House elections and prohibits independent expenditures supporting or opposing House candidates.
Funds the system through voluntary taxpayer designations on tax returns and a 0.1 percentage point increase in the corporate income tax rate (from 35% to 35.1%) on taxable income above $10 million.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations and taxpayers bear the cost. The bill raises the corporate tax rate from 35% to 35.1% on income over $10 million to fund the public financing pool, and taxpayers can voluntarily direct a portion of their tax refunds or add contributions to the fund. Corporations pay more in taxes, and all taxpayers fund the system whether or not they use the checkoff.

drawbacks.text: The spending caps and funding formula would severely restrict how much money campaigns can raise and spend, which could disadvantage candidates who lack name recognition or an incumbent's free media coverage, making it harder to mount a competitive challenge.

The ban on independent expenditures in House elections would be constitutionally questionable; a ban on independent spending by outside groups would almost certainly face a First Amendment challenge under Supreme Court precedent (Buckley v. Valeo), and the bill anticipates this by providing an expedited procedure for a constitutional amendment if struck down.
Public financing shifts the cost of campaigns from private donors to the general taxpayer and corporations, meaning people who do not participate in elections still help pay for them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem: the dominance of private money in congressional elections. Public financing with spending caps would reduce candidates' dependence on wealthy donors and could broaden who runs for office. The costs are real but modest: a 0.1% corporate surcharge and voluntary taxpayer contributions. The biggest honest concern is legal viability and enforceability, not cost: the bill's own authors built in a constitutional amendment trigger, acknowledging that key provisions would likely be struck down. It never advanced far enough to test any of this in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to three committees but never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; it died at the end of the 105th Congress.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 7, 1997, and referred to the House Oversight, Ways and Means, and Rules Committees.
On February 24, 1997, it was referred to a subcommittee on Rules and Organization of the House, where no further action was taken.
The bill had zero cosponsors and no further legislative action occurred before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress, who benefit from the existing private-donor campaign finance system, are better off because the bill never advanced; the status quo of private campaign funding was preserved for another two years.

against.name: House Oversight Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its January 1997 referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Rules Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred to subcommittee in February 1997; no further action taken.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no cosponsors and no recorded votes, so its partisan support is unclear; it died in committee without reaching the floor.

industries.industry: Large corporations and major campaign donors
industries.note: The bill would have raised corporate tax rates slightly to fund public elections and banned soft money contributions, reducing the leverage of large donors over House members. Corporations lose a small tax advantage and donors lose influence over elected officials.

industries.industry: Political consulting and campaign advertising industry
industries.note: Hard spending caps and a ban on independent expenditures would shrink the market for paid political advertising and consulting in House races. This industry profits from unrestricted campaign spending.
